extraction.interpretation: Identifies the protagonist through a colonial-era cultural and social identity.
Locates the narrative in a hill station associated with British colonial presence in India. This association is contextual rather than an explicit statement in the story.
Invokes Rudyard Kipling and establishes a historical frame associated with British colonial India.

extraction.lexical_item: the school had been run on English public school lines
extraction.interpretation: Explicitly identifies the adoption of the English public-school educational model in an Indian institution.
Identifies the students within the institution shaped by English educational conventions. The word itself is not independently colonial.
Indicates the participation of economically privileged Indian families in a British-model educational institution.
Represents the adoption of British public-school dress conventions.
Introduces an American publication as an external cultural reference. Its presence alone does not establish colonial domination.
Compares an Indian school with the prestigious English institution Eton, suggesting the symbolic authority of British educational models.
Reintroduces the uniform as a marker of institutional identity. Its postcolonial relevance derives from the earlier description of the English-model school.
A colonial-era honorific used by the watchman when addressing Mr Oliver, indicating a hierarchical relationship and inherited colonial forms of address.
Represents a subordinate institutional position in contrast with the teacher's social authority. The occupational term itself is not inherently colonial.
The protagonist occupies an institutional authority position within the English-model school. Its postcolonial significance depends on the surrounding educational context.
